metadata.title: Educational mismatch and wages: Evidence from a cross-country comparison

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses OECD’s PIAAC microdata (2011–2014, first two rounds) restricted to employed workers aged 16–65 and excludes self-employed workers. The manuscript does not report applying PIAAC sampling weights or any replicate-weight variance estimation; therefore, the analysis should be treated as unweighted with respect to complex survey design unless the authors used weights implicitly (not stated). Because the core identification strategy is propensity score matching and Heckman two-step selection correction, analysts should verify whether PIAAC design weights (and any replicate weights) were applied in the estimation software; if not, standard errors may not fully reflect the survey’s clustering/stratification. The paper also applies within-country winsorization of hourly wages, job tenure, and work experience at the 1st and 99th percentiles, which is a preprocessing step that can affect tails but is distinct from survey-weighting.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This paper does not use PISA/TIMSS-style plausible values for cognitive achievement as an outcome; instead, it uses PIAAC directly assessed numeracy scores and constructs mismatch indicators and wage outcomes. While the authors state that they use the first plausible value from PIAAC’s multiple imputation procedure for the numeracy-based skill mismatch benchmark, they do not provide a complete, auditable description of the missing-data handling procedure (e.g., imputation model details, number of imputations, and how uncertainty is propagated). This is therefore a reporting gap for missing-data transparency rather than a design-driven non-applicability.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Uses PIAAC data from the first two survey rounds (2011–2014). Restricts the analytic sample to employed workers aged 16–65, excluding individuals in school-to-work transitions. Excludes self-employed workers due to measurement concerns about reported earnings and ambiguous job-education requirements. Winsorizes hourly wages, job tenure, and work experience at the 1st and 99th percentiles within each country to reduce outlier influence. For mismatch measurement, classifies overeducation/undereducation using self-assessed required education (main analysis) and constructs realized-match (RM) alternatives using occupational education distributions (mean-based and mode-based) at the one-digit ISCO level. For skill mismatch, uses PIAAC numeracy scores relative to occupation-specific medians and standard deviations, and distinguishes genuine vs apparent overeducation using the joint educational and skill mismatch criteria.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIAAC 2011–2014 (Rounds 1–2) employed workers aged 16–65 — wage analysis
main_findings.performance_metrics: Heckman two-step baseline (pooled): −0.138 (men: −0.126; women: −0.143). PSM (kernel matching, KM) country examples: Britain −0.366 (overeducation, KM), Japan −0.196, Korea −0.219, Slovakia −0.073; pooled PSM ATT reported as 13.8% penalty.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC 2011–2014 (Rounds 1–2) employed workers aged 16–65 the study leveraged overeducation status alongside attained education, numeracy skill score, and parental education to estimate the wage penalty of overeducation, finding that overeducated workers earn about 13.8% less than appropriately matched workers in pooled cross-national observations. This indicates that reducing credential-job mismatch—especially in institutional contexts where penalties remain large—may improve labor-market efficiency and earnings, though the estimates rely on matching/selection corrections rather than randomized assignment.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIAAC 2011–2014 (Rounds 1–2) employed workers aged 16–65 — wage analysis
main_findings.performance_metrics: Heckman two-step baseline (pooled): 0.099 (men: 0.113; women: 0.075). PSM (KM) country examples: Chile 0.225, Britain 0.181, Japan 0.172, Israel −0.010, Greece −0.008; pooled PSM ATT reported as 9.9% premium.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC 2011–2014 (Rounds 1–2) employed workers aged 16–65 the study leveraged undereducation status alongside attained education, numeracy skill score, and experience-related controls to estimate the wage premium of undereducation, finding that undereducated workers earn about 9.9% more than appropriately matched workers in pooled cross-national observations. This indicates that policies should not treat all undereducation as purely harmful; instead, they should support pathways that allow skills and experience to translate into productivity and wages, while recognizing that selection into undereducation is addressed via matching rather than experimental design.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIAAC 2011–2014 (Rounds 1–2) employed workers aged 16–65 — mediation analysis
main_findings.target_variable: Mediated share of overeducation/undereducation effects through mechanisms
main_findings.performance_metrics: Mediation (Table 5): Overeducation—proportion mediated: occupational sorting 0.052, supervisory positions 0.055, task autonomy 0.026, work method discretion 0.032, ICT skills 0.080, influencing skills 0.087, writing skills 0.057. Undereducation—proportion mediated: occupational sorting 0.104, supervisory positions 0.106, task autonomy 0.051, work method discretion 0.044, ICT skills 0.143, influencing skills 0.114, writing skills 0.086.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC 2011–2014 (Rounds 1–2) employed workers aged 16–65 the study leveraged overeducation/undereducation status and mechanism variables such as occupational sorting, work flexibility, and ICT/influencing/writing skill utilization to decompose wage effects, finding that occupational sorting and especially cognitive skill utilization mediate a meaningful share of mismatch wage penalties and premiums. This indicates that labor-market interventions should target both job allocation (mobility and hierarchy access) and opportunities to deploy complex skills at work, rather than focusing only on credential attainment.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIAAC 2011–2014 (Rounds 1–2) employed workers aged 16–65 — genuine vs apparent overeducation decomposition
main_findings.target_variable: Genuine vs apparent overeducation wage penalties
top_predictors: Job satisfaction (proxy via mismatch type Method 2)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Genuine vs apparent overeducation (Table 11, SA Method 1): average genuine −19.0% vs apparent −14.5% (gap 4.5 pp). SA Method 2 (job satisfaction-based): genuine −21.6% vs apparent −13.2% (gap 8.0 pp). Country examples (SA Method 1): Britain genuine −40.6% vs apparent −29.2%; Netherlands −31.4% vs −16.1%; Slovenia −23.1% vs −15.8%.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC 2011–2014 (Rounds 1–2) employed workers aged 16–65 the study leveraged overeducation status together with numeracy-based skill mismatch (and job satisfaction in an alternative decomposition) to distinguish genuine from apparent overeducation, finding that genuine overeducation imposes substantially larger wage penalties than apparent overeducation across countries. This indicates that policy should prioritize improving real skill-job alignment and productivity utilization (not just credential matching), because credential surplus without capability underutilization is associated with smaller earnings losses.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses OECD’s PIAAC microdata from the first two survey rounds (2011–2014), restricting to employed workers aged 16–65 and excluding self-employed individuals. Educational mismatch is measured as overeducation/undereducation using self-assessed required education (main analysis), with realized-match alternatives based on occupational education distributions; skill mismatch is benchmarked using PIAAC numeracy scores and used to decompose genuine vs apparent overeducation. Baseline Heckman two-step estimates show pooled wage penalties of −13.8% for overeducation and premiums of +9.9% for undereducation, with larger overeducation penalties for women (−14.3%) than men (−12.6%). Propensity score matching (NNM/RM/KM) reveals substantial cross-country heterogeneity, with the largest overeducation penalties in Britain, Cyprus, and Japan and smaller penalties in Nordic countries. Mediation analysis indicates occupational sorting and cognitive skill utilization (ICT/influencing/writing) explain meaningful shares of mismatch wage effects. Limitations include lack of reported survey-weight usage and reliance on matching/selection corrections rather than randomized assignment.
